findings.title: Supply chain vulnerability via dynamic execution of @latest npm package
findings.description: The script uses `npx -y 9router@latest`, which dynamically downloads and executes the newest version of the package. If the `9router` package on npm is compromised, malicious code will be automatically executed by `launchd`/`systemd` as the user.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker compromises the `9router` npm package and publishes a malicious version. Upon machine reboot or service restart, `npx` fetches the compromised `@latest` version and executes it, granting the attacker a reverse shell or stealing `~/.config/sops` keys.
findings.recommendation: Pin the package to a specific version (e.g., `npx -y 9router@1.2.3`) or better yet, package `9router` natively in Nix to ensure reproducibility and hash verification.
findings.confidence_reason: The code explicitly requests `@latest` and executes it directly via a service manager without hash verification.

findings.title: Command injection risk in eval statement
findings.description: The documentation suggests `eval $(sops -d --output-type dotenv secrets/shared/api-keys.yaml)`. If an attacker can modify the encrypted `api-keys.yaml` to include malicious bash commands (e.g., `API_KEY=123; rm -rf /`), it will be executed by the user's shell.
findings.exploit_scenario: A malicious insider or compromised teammate commits a tampered `api-keys.yaml` containing shell commands. When another developer runs the recommended `eval` command to export keys, the shell executes the injected code.
findings.recommendation: Use `set -a; source <(sops -d secrets/shared/api-keys.yaml); set +a` or read variables safely without `eval`.
findings.confidence_reason: This is in documentation, not a script that runs automatically. Furthermore, the attacker would already need commit access to the repo.
